The data will be among the factors that the Bank of Japan will scrutinise when its board produces fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts at this month's policy meeting. The rise in the corporate goods price index, which measures the price companies charge each other for their goods and services, compared with the median market forecast for a 7.6% increase. It slowed from a 7.6% gain in August. The yen-based import price index surged 24.5% in September from a year earlier, the data released by the BOJ showed, a sign that the currency's weakness continued to push up the cost of raw material imports. "Wholesale inflation will likely re-accelerate given strong uncertainty over the Middle East conflict, which is keeping crude oil prices elevated," said Masato Koike, a senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. "But there's no sign of inflationary pressure accelerating sharply for the time being," heightening the chance that the BOJ will stand pat in October and wait until December to raise interest rates again, he said. Speaking in parliament on Tuesday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda [USN:SPN45900V TEXT:"said"] underlying inflation "has now come quite close to 2%." Unlike in the past, when the aim of monetary policy was to lift underlying inflation toward 2%, Ueda said the economy "has entered a phase where an important policy objective is to keep it stable at around that level." On Tuesday, a separate BOJ survey [USN:P8N45R035 TEXT:"showed"] that the ratio of Japanese households expecting prices to rise five years from now increased to 86.5% from 86.1% in the previous survey in June, suggesting inflation expectations remain firmly entrenched. At the same time, the pace of expected inflation moderated, with households projecting prices to rise by an average of 11.8% in a year's time, down from 13.1%, and by 10.1% annually over the next five years, compared with 10.8% in the previous survey. BOJ EYES PASS-THROUGH A recent spike in wholesale inflation was among the factors that the BOJ cited as evidence of mounting price pressures behind its decision to raise interest rates in June and September. While the prices of farm products fell 13.3% in September from a year earlier due largely to plunging prices for rice, a broad range of other goods recorded price rises, including processed food, electric machinery and telecommunications equipment, the data showed. Prices of chemical goods rose 13.3%, plastic products increased 12.8% and non-ferrous metals goods were up 40.2%, a sign of the increasing cost firms were facing from the weak yen, the US-Israeli war on Iran and robust AI-related demand, the data showed. Governor Ueda has said the key to the pace and timing of future rate hikes would be the extent to which such upward pressure on wholesale prices spreads to consumer inflation, as well as how that could affect consumption. Recent data showed [USN:L4N45M0C3 TEXT:"core consumer inflation in Tokyo"], which is considered a leading indicator of nationwide price trends, accelerated in September at its fastest pace in 10 months. [USN:L4N45S011 TEXT:"Sources have told Reuters"] the BOJ may signal this month that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2% target, highlighting its readiness to raise rates again in the coming months. The BOJ raised its key rate to a 31-year high [USN:L1N459138 TEXT:"last month"], while signalling its entry into a phase focused on preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its target, raising the prospect of tighter policy. At the meeting on October 29 and 30, the BOJ will release fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts that will be closely watched by market participants for clues to the timing of the next rate hike. [USN:L4N44Z0P0 TEXT:"Many analysts"] expect the central bank to raise interest rates again by the end of this year.

item.title: Reporters accuse India of crackdown on journalists, press freedom at youth-led protests
item.description: Nearly three dozen journalists were detained for hours before being released.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Chaturvedi, Shivangi Acharya, Saurabh Sharma
item.content:encoded: Police used excessive and targeted force on journalists covering youth-led protests in India, local press groups and international media rights bodies said, and warned that press freedom in the country was under threat. Young Indians, mobilised by the "cockroach" youth movement and supported by opposition parties, took to the streets of New Delhi on the weekend demanding [USN:L6N45Y06O TEXT:"the resignation"] of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a sharply contested revision of voter lists in the country. They allege the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party in the elections, a charge the Election Commission denies. Nearly three dozen journalists from outlets including the Indian Express, Scroll and Newslaundry, were detained for hours before being released, according to Reuters interviews with some journalists. Some were dragged and roughly handled by the police and their phones were seized, according to a Reuters reporter at the scene, journalists interviewed by Reuters, and footage from mainstream and digital news outlets. Some of those detained said they were clearly identifiable as members of the press. The Reuters journalist was also briefly detained. The Delhi police did not immediately reply to an e-mailed request for comment on how many journalists were detained and why, and how they were handled by officers. Earlier, police said in a video posted on X that some protesters had posed as journalists and had interfered with their work. The government did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "The actions of the Indian authorities during the recent student protests, led by the Cockroach Janta Party, demonstrate how their tactics are designed to stifle media coverage and can be combined to suppress journalism," said Ritika Jain, India representative of Reporters Without Borders. "Detention, surveillance, internet shutdowns, and the removal of journalistic content form a chain of restrictions," she said, urging authorities to remove restrictions on journalists. COURT RULED POLICE SHOULD NOT IMPEDE REPORTERS The police action led lawyers to seek a ruling from India's top court on Sunday to allow lawyers and journalists to perform their duties, with the court ruling in favour. However, some detentions came after the court order, journalists said. Press Club of India, the nation's largest journalist group, called the police action "a blatant attack on the freedom of press." In a joint statement with three other bodies, it said journalists were held while they were filming the police detaining protesters and their devices were seized. The associations also sought a formal apology and investigation into the actions of senior police officials. "I was interviewing some people detained in a bus when a police officer came at me and grabbed my mic...I was dragged, my phone was snatched and I was forcefully detained along with my producer," Anmol Pritam, a reporter at Indian digital news outlet Newslaundry, told Reuters. He was detained for nearly three hours on October 10. Police did not respond to a request for comment on the case. India ranks 157 out of 180 countries in the press freedom index of Reporters Without Borders, having fallen from 133 a decade ago. Critics attribute the drop to the Modi government's increased attempts to restrain the press and shrink space for critical or dissenting voices in its 12-year rule. The Indian government has often denied the claim. The Indian government did not immediately respond to a request for comment e-mailed outside usual work hours. The Indian constitution recognises journalists' rights under free speech provisions but also allows authorities to impose reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order.

item.title: What's in the diesel deal between Putin and Trump?
item.description: US President Donald Trump has stepped up his efforts to lower US diesel prices by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports and announcing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump has stepped up his efforts to lower US diesel prices by lifting sanctions on Russian [USN:L1N45V0MW TEXT:"diesel exports"] and announcing a [USN:L1N45X021 TEXT:"ceasefire"] on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine. Soaring US diesel prices are hurting US truckers and farmers, and are a [USN:L6N4571B5 TEXT:"concern for voters"] and political parties ahead of November 3 midterm elections . US prices were down 0.5% on Monday following Trump's announcements. HOW MUCH DIFFERENCE WILL RUSSIA'S RELEASE MAKE? Trump said on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets. That is less than a day's supply for the US transport sector alone, according to US Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels per day. Trump said Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons "immediately thereafter", which is less than four days' demand for US transport. WHAT HURDLES MIGHT THERE BE? The US has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports, but it remains unclear what tankers could be used to export the fuel given sanctions on many, and what the condition is of Russian refineries given recent Ukrainian attacks on them. HOW MUCH CAN RUSSIA EXPORT? Russia was capable of exporting about 100,000 tons of diesel per day prior to Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries that began in 2024. In light of damage to its refineries, Russia banned [USN:L8N45M0AV TEXT:"diesel exports"] from July to meet domestic demand and extended that ban to countries without bilateral agreements until October 31, while sustaining steady exports to "friendly" states, mostly in Central Asia. If Ukraine halts [USN:L6N45T0GE TEXT:"attacks"] on Russian refineries, Russia would be capable of meeting the initial request from Trump for 300,000 tons of diesel exports, according to industry sources. Russia could produce 300,000 tons of diesel this month if a large oil refinery hit by drones in the European part of the country were to restart, the sources said. WILL MORE DIESEL EXPORTS HELP RUSSIA'S ECONOMY? According to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries cost Russia's economy 1% of gross domestic product, which is around $26.6 billion, according to Reuters calculations. Exports of 300,000 tons of diesel would fetch roughly $400 million, of which a small portion would go to Russia's state budget. Russia taxes mostly oil output, not oil and fuel exports. Russia has around 30 large oil refineries, while none are functioning in Ukraine. WHAT’S BEEN THE REACTION TO TRUMP'S ANNOUNCEMENTS? Moscow said on Saturday it had [USN:S8N42200X TEXT:"partially lifted"] the ban on diesel exports in place since July with immediate effect. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Trump's diesel supply deal with Russia would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine and cost more lives. US lawmakers also criticised the move, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not lift them. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country [USN:FWN45V15A TEXT:"would strengthen"] its sanctions on Russia. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul restated Berlin's support for Ukraine’s leader after Trump called for his removal, and called for more pressure to be put on Russia to resume peace talks. The Kremlin said on Monday the talks were continuing on the ceasefire, while declining to comment on whether that is related only to oil refineries. CHINA'S IMPACT ON DIESELChina is set to [USN:L1N45V02I TEXT:"resume refined fuel exports"] after a brief halt during the Golden Week holiday, Reuters reported. However, its approved October exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel, at around 3.7 million metric tons, are down sharply from a year earlier and lower than the more than 4 million approved for September. WHY HAVE DIESEL PRICES BEEN SO TIGHT? In addition to Russian export challenges, the Iran war has curbed supply from Gulf producers. IEA SPURRING MORE SUPPLY The Group of Seven nations agreed recently to [USN:L6N45T0GQ TEXT:"release"] fuel from their strategic reserves, coordinated by the International Energy Agency. The 32-nation IEA coordinated the world's largest emergency stocks release in March of over 400 million barrels of crude oil and products, and has recently prodded participating countries to offer any unreleased volumes to market.

item.title: Broadcom CEO sees capital hurdle to AI growth, 'casino' in AI investing
item.description: Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said on Monday that capital will be the biggest constraint facing the company as AI development continues and likened some of the investment flow into the broader sector to "casino gambling".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Broadcom (AVGO.O) CEO Hock Tan said on Monday that capital will be the biggest constraint facing the company as AI development continues and likened some of the investment flow into the broader sector to "casino gambling". At a panel in Singapore on Monday, Tan said that the company is overcoming wafer shortages and memory shortages, but capital will be the biggest constraint He added that frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI have shown that they can generate significant revenue from the latest models that have been deployed for AI personal assistants "A lot of investors have no clue what they're investing in, but set very extreme expectations, only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino gambling," he said, when asked about the impact of cheaper AI models
